Register your app

Before a member can sign in on your site, WallFlowers registers it: which community it shows, where its pages are, and where sign-in returns to.

On your machine: nothing to register

For local development, every team uses one shared client, hackathon-local. Serve your page on http://localhost:<port> or http://127.0.0.1:<port>, and use one of these as your callback, character for character:

  • http://localhost:<port>/callback, for port 3000–3009
  • http://localhost:<port>/, for port 3000–3009, 5173–5175, 8000, 8080

The same on 127.0.0.1. They are different origins: a member signed in on one is not signed in on the other.

When a member signs in, WallFlowers asks which of their communities your page may use: the ones they own or administer. The session reaches that community and nothing else. Someone who owns or administers none is told so ("you are the owner or an admin of no Site"), and must make one first at wallflowers.io/signup. Already have a WallFlowers account? Press Create my account, then, on the next page, choose Sign in with a passkey, so the community is made for the account you already have. Make a test community for the hackathon and choose that one, not a community with real members: your page acts there with your full standing.

This client works only on your own machine. To put your site on the web, register it as below.

1. Make your community

Sign up at wallflowers.io/signup: choose what it is, its name and its address, then, if you are building an app, Your app (its local port, callback path and deployed URL; or Skip), then your account. Already have a WallFlowers account? Press Create my account, then, on the next page, choose Sign in with a passkey, so the community is made for the account you already have. You land in WallFlowers' app, the community's owner. If you filled in Your app, signup shows its Site id afterwards, with Copy, and the request for a deployed URL. Without it: To find its id: while signed in, open https://app.wallflowers.io/v2/graph in a new tab; find the object with "kind": "group" and your community's name; its id is the id beside it. (Its public page, "kind": "host", has the same name: not that one.) If it answers not signed in, sign in to WallFlowers in that browser and reload the tab. Once a member signs in on your site, the same id is session.site.

2. Send your registration

FieldExample
community71c1…6a6cThe community your site shows (its id).
callbackshttp://localhost:5173/The page a member returns to after signing in; one or more. Matched exactly: scheme, host, port, path and trailing slash.
originshttp://localhost:5173Where your pages are served from. List every one: production, a preview, each local port. localhost and 127.0.0.1 are different origins.
home (optional)https://your.site/communityOnly if your community hands out join QR codes (a kiosk): where WallFlowers sends a scanned one, as #join=… (POST /v2/join). On one of your origins.

Send these to the hackathon's organisers.

WallFlowers gives you back your client id. A session from your site reaches that community and nothing else.

Teams: adding a teammate

A community has one owner. To build together, the owner adds each teammate to it:

  1. The teammate makes a WallFlowers account at https://app.wallflowers.io (Create an account), then opens Your card (the profile menu, or https://app.wallflowers.io/#you) and, under Your contact code, presses Copy a new code. They send the code to the owner.
  2. The owner opens the community in WallFlowers, then its settings (the round badge beside its name), Add by contact code, pastes it into Contact code, and presses Add. The teammate joins the community and up to five of its rooms, in the community's order; for each room past five, the owner's app says "room: needs another code".
  3. The teammate signs in on your site: they now reach the same community. On your own machine, with hackathon-local, the sign-in offers only communities the person owns or administers: the owner first makes the teammate an admin (their card in WallFlowers, Make admin).

A code works once, for 30 minutes: "Used already" or "the contact code has expired" means ask for a new one.

A wrong callback is refused with a 400 that begins "<callback>" is not a callback client "<client>" registered, and an unknown client id with one that begins no client "<client>" is registered. A registration counts within seconds of WallFlowers adding it: the Door reads its list of sites again every 2 s, with no restart, so no one is signed out. It does not change the sign-in script or its hash.
